new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic (minor syllable + main syllable); stress falls on the main syllable, i.e. the word-final syllable. This is stated for West Bahnaric languages as a group (Sapuan is one of the languages profiled from the authors' own fieldwork); the Sapuan profile adds only that minor-syllable vowels are fully vocalised ('noticeable prominence'), as in Oi, not that they bear stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the Sapuan-specific remark that minor-syllable vowels receive 'noticable prominence' (clear [a]-like vocalisation, as in Oi) concerns vowel realisation rather than stress placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (mono- or sesquisyllabic lexical word); statement is branch-level (West Bahnaric / PWB), not a Sapuan-specific sentence.
new_statements.identity_note: PL-551 sec. 3.6 describes Sapuan of Ban Sapuan (c. 40 km north of Attapeu, Sekong valley), autonym Səpuar = Glottolog sapu1248 / ISO spu; single-village language. The quoted stress sentence (p.33) is a West-Bahnaric-wide statement, not Sapuan-specific.

sources.note: Sec. 3.6 'Sapuan' pp.24-25 (PDF 34-35): language profile from the authors' fieldwork + Ferlus 1969-70 wordlist; inventories (Tables 3.17-3.18); 'Phonologically Sapuan is similar to Oi, generally losing glottalisation, leniting some mainsyllable initials, and giving noticable prominence to minorsyllable vowels' -- no Sapuan-specific stress-placement sentence. Sec. 4.2 'PWB phonological word' p.33 (PDF 43): 'Most WB languages are sesquisyllabic.. a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable' = word-final (main-syllable) stress stated for West Bahnaric languages generally.
